item.title: Collateral Equilibrium with a Continuum of States and No Ex Post Survival Assumption
item.description: arXiv:2611.10019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existence results for incomplete markets with a continuum of states require ex post incomes to be nonnegative, or endowments to be bounded away from zero in every state. Such conditions rule out disaster states, in which some agents receive no income at all. We show that, with a single good and collateralized securities in the sense of Geanakoplos and Zame, an equilibrium exists when second-period endowments are arbitrary nonnegative functions of the state: they may vanish on any set of states, including all of them. Only first-period endowments are required to be positive; no survival assumption is imposed ex post. The reason is that non-recourse collateral makes every portfolio solvent in every state, and with one good this is all the limit argument needs.
item.dc:creator: Jaime Orrillo

item.title: Analysis of Supply Information, Code Bidding, and Efficiency in Repetitive Simultaneous Ascending Online Auctions: A Study of India's eNAM Digital Agricultural Market
item.description: arXiv:2611.10068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analyzes a Repetitive Simultaneous Ascending Auction (RSAA) mechanism employed in India's eNAM digital agricultural market. RSAA is characterized by full seasonal supply transparency and a strategic seller option to reject equilibrium bids. We develop a model of the RSAA game with inter-round strategic dependence and endogenous seller entry, and we find conditions for collusion formation. Using transaction-level data, we empirically validate the emergence of code bidding, a tacit collusive strategy sustained by low bidder concentration and shared supply information. The results show that demand-side coordination systematically reduces price competition. Moreover, the coexistence of supply transparency and strategic rejection introduces significant allocative inefficiencies despite the ascending-price format. These findings offer novel insights for auctions and market design, particularly concerning collusion vulnerability and efficiency in agricultural and digital commodity markets.
item.dc:creator: Dipankar Das, Kingshuk Sarkar, Vivek Jadhav

item.title: When Is Mediated Communication Possible?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when players can truthfully share private information through a mediator. Our analysis focuses on symmetric linear-quadratic games with strategic complements and independent private values. We characterize when mediated communication is informative, meaning that it can induce an outcome different from the unique Bayes-Nash outcome without communication. A sharp dichotomy emerges. When types that prefer higher own actions benefit less from higher opponent actions, informative communication is impossible regardless of the type distribution. By contrast, when those types benefit more from higher opponent actions, informative communication is possible if and only if the relevant extreme type lies sufficiently far from the mean. In a linear-demand Bertrand oligopoly, informative communication is impossible under private costs but may arise under private demand. Finally, informative communication weakly benefits every type. But whenever information sharing can raise aggregate welfare, the maximum aggregate payoff under communication is strictly below the maximum payoff achievable without truth-telling constraints.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Dai, Anna Merotto

item.title: Sequential Candidate Entry: A Counterexample to the Osborne--Kats Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2611.10591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finitely many potential candidates sequentially choose an electoral position on the interval [0,1] or stay out, observing all prior choices. Voters have a uniform distribution of ideal positions on the same interval and vote non-strategically for a nearest candidate; candidates at the same position divide its votes. Candidates with the largest vote share divide a unit payoff equally, losing entrants receive a negative payoff, and staying out yields zero. In the mid-1980s, Osborne and Kats conjectured that, for every number $n\geq 2$ of players, the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) outcome has only the first and last players entering at the median. We refute the conjecture by establishing the existence of a different SPNE outcome for 12 players. Starting from the first two entries proposed earlier by de Vries, we select an SPNE strategy profile after the first two locations 1/2 and 1/10 that gives the second player payoff at least 1/10.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Dagaev

item.title: Optimal hybrid tax enforcement
item.description: arXiv:2611.10851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern tax design and enforcement rely on classification data reported by taxpayers. Data improve the targeting of tax policy and audits but also open avenues for evasion. How can tax authorities use such data while accounting for their potential strategic distortion? We demonstrate that restoring deterrence generates an endogenous global verification frontier: every report below the frontier is verified through either a profit audit or data verification. Optimal hybrid tax enforcement requires selecting which data classes are subject to profit audits up to the global frontier and which are profit-audited only up to lower class-specific cutoffs, with data verification taking over beyond these cutoffs. This costly data verification requirement limits the benefit from differentiated tax enforcement. Optimal implementation is characterized by profit bunching but involves no data bunching.
item.dc:creator: Saara H\"am\"al\"ainen, Eduardo Ferraz, Sebasti\'an Castillo Ramos

item.title: Fair Combinatorial Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2611.11143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An efficient and stable auction can leave the seller with no share of the surplus. We study how the gains from a combinatorial auction can be shared as equally as possible between the seller and buyers while respecting coalitional stability. We show that, when buyers are substitutes, the core is described by individual caps on the buyers' payoffs and contains a unique Lorenz-dominant payoff vector. Each buyer receives the seller's payoff capped at her marginal contribution. The seller consequently receives at least an equal share of the total surplus, without compromising efficiency or stability. We then construct a complete-information bargaining game in which the seller proposes a division of the surplus and rejecting buyers receive exit payments. Without discounting, the game fully implements the Lorenz-dominant vector in pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium: an equilibrium exists, and every such equilibrium yields precisely this division.
item.dc:creator: Karan Maniyar

item.title: Distributionally Robust Rational Inattention
item.description: arXiv:2611.11855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a rational inattention model in which a decision maker chooses a stochastic choice rule while facing ambiguity about the prior distribution over states. Ambiguity is modeled through a distributionally robust formulation in which the prior belongs to an uncertainty set defined by a general phi-divergence. Our main result establishes an exact Lagrangian dual representation of the resulting max-min problem as a finite-dimensional concave optimization problem. This characterization yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the emergence of robust consideration sets and a tractable one-dimensional dual representation for the Cressie-Read family of divergences. We further connect the model to robust risk measures: Average Value-at-Risk arises from a particular non-smooth divergence, while Kullback-Leibler ambiguity is linked through Lagrangian duality to the entropic-risk multiplier representation. We then develop two extensions. The first allows the attention-cost technology and prior ambiguity to be governed by distinct phi-divergences, while the second introduces a deeper layer of ambiguity over the decision maker's baseline prior. Both extensions preserve the finite-dimensional structure of the model and encompass standard Kullback-Leibler robust rational inattention specifications as special or corresponding multiplier cases.
item.dc:creator: Emerson Melo

item.title: Separable social welfare evaluation without completeness
item.description: arXiv:2611.11864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study incomplete social evaluation of utility vectors to capture situations in which there is disagreement in society about the degree of inequality aversion. We characterize multi-prioritarian criteria using efficiency, equity, impartiality, separability, and a condition called continuous divisible completion condition. We also provide uniqueness results and investigate comparative inequality aversion.
item.dc:creator: Kaname Miyagishima, Eisuke Uchida, Kenta Yoshida

item.title: Individual incentives and uniform gains under symmetric constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.12151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the division of a fixed total under symmetric joint constraints when agents have continuous, strictly single-peaked preferences over their own shares. Each agent reports a complete preference, including comparisons across the two sides of her peak. For any finite population and any nonempty closed convex permutation-invariant feasible set, we characterize the uniform-gains rule by efficiency, symmetry, individual strategy-proofness, and own-coordinate peak-onlyness. The last condition requires that a change of preference leaving an agent's peak fixed also leave her own share fixed; it places no direct restriction on others' shares. The characterization separates uniqueness from continuity and yields a continuous characterization with individual incentives for compact feasible sets that are polyhedral or relatively full-dimensional and strictly convex. We then show that, for every population of two through six agents and every nonempty compact convex permutation-invariant feasible set, efficiency, symmetry, and individual strategy-proofness alone characterize uniform gains. The proof recovers allocations from the shares attainable by unilateral reports, feasible transfers, and endpoint reports. A common induction applies at each population, with additional starting configurations for five and six agents.
item.dc:creator: Siwei Chen

item.title: Inequality-Aware Regulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I study regulation of a screening monopolist when the regulator cares about the distribution of surplus across heterogeneous consumers and the firm. Consumers privately know their willingness to pay for quality, and the firm privately knows its production costs. Regulatory contracts specify quality-price options that the firm must offer. I show that when the regulator gives greater weight to consumers with lower willingness to pay, baseline regulation is optimal: the regulator requires affordable basic options but leaves the firm free to design and price premium options. Under strong consumer-side redistributive concerns, a single required basic option suffices. The regulator uses the firm's incentive to extract surplus from premium buyers to support low regulated prices for basic options.
item.dc:creator: Mikael M\"akimattila

item.title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Resource Allocation under Institutional Asymmetry
item.description: arXiv:2611.12534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a two-player knapsack game to investigate resource allocation under individual capacity constraints, competition over shared resources, and institutional asymmetry. Players select feasible subsets of resources, while their payoffs depend on competitive losses, allocation rules, and asymmetric institutional benefits and costs. We derive the aggregate welfare function and show that allocation coefficients redistribute payoffs without directly affecting total welfare, whereas institutional parameters influence welfare through their net contribution. Consequently, institutional arrangements with identical welfare effects may induce different strategic incentives and Nash equilibrium outcomes. We analyze how capacity constraints and institutional priority shape equilibrium configurations and their welfare properties. A central result concerns the distinction between the social efficiency and strategic stability of shared resources. We derive conditions under which sharing is socially preferable to exclusive allocation yet remains strategically unstable because the non-priority player can increase their payoff by abandoning the resource. Conversely, sharing may remain strategically stable even when exclusive allocation yields higher aggregate welfare. These findings demonstrate that social efficiency and strategic stability need not coincide under institutional asymmetry.
item.dc:creator: Jorge David Casta\~no-Yepes, Marcela Herrera, Javier Parra-Dom\'inguez

item.title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12343v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Vaccario, Luca Verginer, Frank Schweitzer

item.title: Robust Contracts with Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2212.00157v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a moral hazard problem over an arbitrary finite horizon, with multiple agents whose action sets are unknown to the principal. The principal contracts with the agents sequentially and seeks to maximize the worst-case discounted sum of payoffs, where the worst case is over the possible action sets. The principal observes the action chosen by each agent, and then offers a new contract to the next agent based on the knowledge accumulated so far, thus having the opportunity to explore in every period before the final one. We introduce and compare three different notions of dynamic worst-case evaluation. Within each notion, we define a suitable rule of updating and characterize the principal's optimal payoff guarantee. We find that linear contracts are robustly optimal not only in static settings, but also in dynamic environments with exploration.
item.dc:creator: Chang Liu

item.title: On the Monotonicity of Information Measures
item.description: arXiv:2404.15158v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the monotonicity of information measures, functions that assign a value to each statistical experiment, with respect to the Blackwell and Lehmann orders. We show that such monotonicity can be characterized by local, first-order conditions. Under natural invariance properties, a measure is Blackwell monotone if and only if it decreases in the direction of signal replacements, and Lehmann monotone if and only if it decreases in the direction of reverse signal replacements, which replace signals with higher ones only in low states or with lower ones only in high states. We translate both conditions into the space of posterior beliefs and apply them to likelihood-separable and posterior-separable measures, showing in particular that the entropy cost is Lehmann monotone. Among posterior-separable measures, we further identify a Lehmann monotone subclass, posterior-mean-ratio measures, that characterizes the Lehmann order.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Cheng, Yonggyun Kim

item.title: Disappointment Aversion and Expectiles
item.description: arXiv:2508.05541v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper recasts Gul's (1991) theory of disappointment aversion in a Savage framework, with general outcomes, new explicit axioms of disappointment aversion, and novel explicit representations. These permit broader applications of the theory and a better understanding of its decision-theoretic foundations. Our results exploit an unexpected connection between Gul's model and the econometric framework of Newey and Powell (1987) of asymmetric least squares estimation. Our main axiomatization result shows that a preference relation over Savage acts is probabilistically sophisticated, invariant biseparable, and disappointment hedging if and only if it admits a representation \emph{\`a la} Gul, and hence all explicit equivalent representations that we present in the paper. We also derive a neurocomputational foundation of the theory based on recent neuroscience findings and a novel reinforcement learning result.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Bellini, Fabio Maccheroni, Tiantian Mao, Ruodu Wang, Qinyu Wu

item.title: Random Collection
item.description: arXiv:2511.18476v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies choice situations in which a decision maker can choose multiple alternatives. Given a menu of available options, the decision maker selects a subset of the menu with certain probabilities. We employ an axiomatic approach to characterize various parametric models in the literature. We identify two main behavioral postulates that organize the models into overlapping classes based on their shared behavioral properties. Our results elucidate the implications of the functional form assumptions and shed light on the distinctions between models. The behavioral postulates offer simple tools for testing and falsifying the choice procedures used by the decision maker and reveal a close connection between models that are seemingly unrelated.
item.dc:creator: Tri Phu Vu

item.title: Risk-insurance parity
item.description: arXiv:2512.09208v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Risk aversion and insurance are two prominent and interconnected concepts in economics and finance. To explore their fundamental connection, we introduce risk-insurance parity, which associates various classes of insurance contracts with different notions of risk aversion. We show that the classic notions - both weak and strong - of risk aversion can be characterized by propensity to different classes of insurance contracts, generalizing recent results on propensity to full, proportional, and deductible-limit contracts in the literature. We examine in depth classes of insurance indemnity functions that correspond to weak and strong risk aversion. We show that one proportional-indemnity contract is enough to obtain equivalence with strong risk aversion. Risk-insurance parity allows us to define two new notions of risk aversion, between weak and strong, characterized by insurance propensity to deductible-only and limit-only contracts, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin C\^ot\'e, Ruodu Wang, Qinyu Wu

item.title: Interacting Principal-Agent Games
item.description: arXiv:2602.20281v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many economic environments, multiple principals simultaneously design incentive systems while interacting strategically with one another. The resulting incentive constraints are interdependent: whether a mechanism is incentive compatible for one principal may depend on the mechanisms chosen by the other principals. This interdependence makes exact equilibrium fragile: small changes in one principal's mechanism can alter the incentive-compatible mechanisms available to others. We establish two complementary equilibrium-existence results. First, for environments with multidimensional type, action, and outcome spaces, we show that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a Bayesian-Nash principals' equilibrium under $\varepsilon$-relaxed incentive compatibility: principals best respond exactly over mechanisms whose agents' ex ante expected deviation regret is at most $\varepsilon$. Thus equilibrium existence can be recovered with arbitrarily small expected incentive regret. In contrast to Myerson's quasi-equilibrium, which keeps incentive compatibility exact but relaxes the principals' optimality requirement, this concept keeps principals' optimization exact and relaxes the agents' incentive constraints. Second, motivated by Myerson's nonexistence example, in which each principal has a single privately informed agent, we examine a one-member team-contest specialization of the general model with voluntary participation. This specialization retains the basic structure of Myerson's setting (competing principals, privately informed agents, and interdependent incentive constraints) while imposing primitive conditions under which exact feasibility varies continuously. In this environment, we establish existence of an exact Bayesian-Nash principals' equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Brian Roberson

item.title: Hidden Commitment Power Is Powerless
item.description: arXiv:2606.02769v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A principal who offers a contract may renege when her default option is sufficiently attractive. The size of this temptation, which inversely measures her commitment power, is often the principal's private information. This paper asks how contracting outcomes change under this information asymmetry. Disciplining off-path beliefs with the Intuitive Criterion, I find that every type of principal behaves and earns payoffs as if she were commonly known to have the least commitment power. Hidden commitment power is therefore powerless, although commitment power can be valuable under symmetric information. The result delivers an unambiguous policy lesson on how to mitigate this information asymmetry prior to contracting: only measures that improve the worst case have value. In an application to credit rating, when the cost of a rating system grows with its number of grades, a rating system that sorts issuers into ordered bands is optimal, and each issuer contracts on the terms warranted by the floor of her band.
item.dc:creator: Hongcheng Li

item.title: On the construction and representation of social welfare orders satisfying consequentialist equity axioms
item.description: arXiv:2606.23428v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we examine the constructive nature of social welfare orders on infinite utility streams $X=Y^{\mathbb{N}}$ satisfying Strong Equity, Hammond Equity, or the Pigou--Dalton transfer principle. The constructive social welfare orders are described using lexicographic preference relations. Social welfare orders satisfying Strong Equity, Hammond Equity, or the Pigou--Dalton transfer principle admit explicit descriptions when $Y(<)$ is well-ordered. We describe restrictions on the domain $Y$ under which the existence of social welfare orders satisfying the aforementioned equity axioms entails the existence of a non-Ramsey collection. For this, we rely on the existence of a non-Ramsey collection, which is treated here as a nonconstructive object.
item.dc:creator: Ram Sewak Dubey, Giorgio Laguzzi

item.title: Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games with Planned Actions and Scouting
item.description: arXiv:2609.17608v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Stag Hunt games in which every action requires planning and preparation. Before players act, they observe noisy signals of their opponent's preparations and can revise their plans, which allows players to screen for cooperation. As screening becomes more precise and cheap, small trembles ensure that, in every equilibrium, play yields the payoff-dominant outcome with a probability that converges to one, even when the safe, low payoff equilibrium is risk dominant. Across scenarios, we emphasize that decomposing an action into (i) preparation and (ii) execution allows us to analyze simultaneous-move games in which players partially observe each other's contemporaneous actions.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Kuhle

item.title: Delegation without Priors
item.description: arXiv:2609.35156v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A principal makes decisions relying on the private information held by a biased agent. Lacking a prior over the circumstances that may arise, she seeks a delegation rule that minimizes worst-case regret relative to the complete-information benchmark. The optimal delegation mechanism governs two distinct margins: whether to depart from a common default action, and how much discretion to grant conditional on departure. This rule pairs the default action with an action gap, followed by a discretionary interval with randomized boundaries designed to balance regret across states. This structure is globally optimal within the class of all stochastic, incentive-compatible mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Wei He, Fei Li, Jiangtao Li, Terrence McGovern, Jan Benedikt Napp, Hanqing Ye, Wenjun Zheng

item.title: Information Divergence and Endogenous Evolution of Asymmetric Information
item.description: arXiv:2610.11200v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard theories trace information asymmetry to privately held information, heterogeneous signals, or costly information acquisition. We identify a distinct mechanism: otherwise identical rational agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times can hold different predictive distributions because their information differs in age. When the transition kernel separates information ages, independent Bernoulli observation arrivals make such divergence recur infinitely often almost surely, even with identical arrival probabilities. When agents instead choose costly updating intensities, independent update realizations can regenerate heterogeneous information ages among ex ante identical agents. In a stationary Gaussian AR(1) environment, the consequences depend on common staleness as well as the age gap: holding the gap fixed, older information raises individual uncertainty while reducing expected squared forecast disagreement and the value of certifying relative freshness. This generates stale consensus: low disagreement despite high uncertainty. With multiple ordered ages, costly certification supports partial-unraveling equilibria in which fresher types certify and sufficiently stale types pool. Under geometric information ages, more frequent updating weakly lowers the smallest and largest equilibrium disclosure cutoffs wherever positive-certification equilibria exist. The framework has implications for credit, insurance, financial markets, and multi-agent AI.
item.dc:creator: Ratna K. Shrestha (University of British Columbia), Gaurav Subedi (RALP Technologies), Ayush Shrestha (Independent Researcher)

item.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.15786v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. We show that the optimal mechanism frontloads the review's information value: the principal's expected payoff is strictly higher in the first period than in the second, even though she is better informed after the review. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation does not preserve the initial ranking of projects and, under a mild condition, declines with quality near the top.
item.dc:creator: Yijun Liu

item.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design with Endogenous Information and Hidden Actions
item.description: arXiv:2611.05692v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design along two dimensions: joint endogeneity and interaction of hidden actions, information acquisition, information production, learning, and disclosure; and generality across economic environments and feasibility structures. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint consistent perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish a dynamic revelation principle under this concept, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. In a private-values environment, we characterize joint incentives through choice optimality, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, global integral monotonicity, and history-report incentives. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, conditional revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions and branched outcomes. We characterize feasible and optimal disclosure. Applications show the Milgrom-Weber revenue ranking can reverse with endogenous information acquisition, while optimal financial-contract disclosure may be absent, interior, or complete.
item.dc:creator: Guoqiang Tian

item.title: Welfare, Improvability, and Variance: A Principal-Agent Approach to Optimal Benchmark Item Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2605.30916v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI benchmarks have well-documented limitations, with prior work examining contamination, saturation, and construct underspecification. Aggregation has received far less attention: benchmarks are typically summarized by uniformly averaging item-level scores, implicitly treating every test item as equally valuable. We model benchmarking as a multitask principal-agent game and show that the welfare loss from a benchmark is determined jointly by three item-level primitives: alignment with normative welfare priorities, marginal improvability, and performance variance. We translate the theory into an audit framework that ranks items along each of these three axes, and apply it to OLMES items using WORKBank for welfare, the EvoLM 4B suite for improvability, and the PolyPythias 410M panel for variance. The framework surfaces items that are Pareto-inferior within OLMES subject to a pro-worker welfare operationalization. All code is available at https://github.com/stair-lab/principal-agent-benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Haupt, Justin Hartenstein, Anka Reuel, Mykel Kochenderfer, Sanmi Koyejo

item.title: Ever since Ellsberg
item.description: arXiv:2607.09355v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ellsberg's famous paradox challenged Savage's subjective expected utility theory (EUT) -- which reduces uncertainty to risk -- by suggesting an aversion toward ambiguity. We provide a revealed preference test of the full set of axioms underpinning subjective EUT under uncertainty and compare it to an analogous test of objective EUT under risk. We find that individual choices are as consistent with utility maximization and expected utility maximization under uncertainty as they are under risk. Nevertheless, there is greater empirical scope for non-EUT models under uncertainty than under risk, and the absolute and relative consistency of EUT and non-EUT models vary considerably across subjects.
item.dc:creator: Aluma Dembo, Shachar Kariv, Matthew Polisson, John K. -H. Quah
